A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same performative-learning framework and job-seeker case study. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original analyses of historical job-seeker data and a semi-simulation, including logistic-regression performance, observed changes, numerical bounds, and policy-sweep results.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C retain the original historical-data analysis and semi-simulation, including predictive performance and computed bounds. The historical bound calculation is revised.

M1.justification: Repeated risk minimization, repeated empirical risk minimization, and the regularized logistic-regression procedure are retained. Revisions concern mathematical assumptions and guarantees rather than a new training or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same German administrative data, the 60,147-person historical cohort, and the 41,585-person semi-simulation cohort for unemployment prediction and job-training allocation. The routing example remains illustrative rather than an evaluated task.

E2.justification: Neither version adds or removes an evaluated external comparator. Both illustrate the same logistic model and the bound variants from Theorems 3.13 and 3.15; additional literature citations are not experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4 revises the reported semi-simulation timing: v1 sets t=0 at day 60 and t=1 fourteen days later, whereas v3 sets t=1 at day 60. Cohort sizes, preprocessing, model settings, and the policy sweep remain unchanged. This documentation change does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Both retain the response-rate sweep, decomposition of the same two bounds, and supplementary illustration under weaker regularity assumptions. Figures 1.3 and 2 contain unchanged plots; no new ablation, robustness test, or supplementary case study appears.

E5.justification: Lemma 3.9 changes the response-rate upper bound's normal quantile from 1−δ/2 to 1−δ. The historical calculation changes δ from 0.1 to 0.025 under the revised confidence formula to retain nominal 95% confidence. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty or seed information.

E6.justification: Appendix B.2 in v1 reports a historical bound of 0.302582; Appendix C.2 in v3 reports 0.307112, with both component values revised. This is a revised analytical calculation with changed confidence calibration, not a predictive-performance deterioration. The reported AUC range and plotted results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds compactness of the data domain, convexity of the parameter space, and explicit data-Lipschitzness of the loss. It replaces the implicit-function argument with a Lipschitz-minimizer proof, revises the shift recursion to involve ε(1+L_a), changes sampling exponents from p/ν to 1/ν, and revises probability guarantees throughout. Response-count and entropy definitions also change. These substantially revise the central mathematical results and proofs.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain bounds under sample and population performativity, the change–learn trade-off, the self-fulfilling/self-negating worst case, and using shifted samples to estimate population responses. The new PLT terminology and conclusion restate these contributions without adding a distinct central claim.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 replaces the earlier εκ/γ-based convergence and stability comparison with a fixed-T interpretation and exponential, linear, or bounded growth governed by ε(1+L_a). Section 3 also adds substantive motivation for Wasserstein sensitivity. The main interpretations and strong-convexity limitation remain.

D1.justification: The stated replication-code location changes from an anonymous repository to the authors' GitHub repository. Restricted-data access instructions, software, regularization, and preprocessing details are substantially retained; the PDFs alone do not verify repository availability.

R1.justification: New citations contextualize Wasserstein sensitivity, including Kim and Perdomo, Jagadeesan et al., and Jin et al. Appendix B extends the existing exploration–exploitation analogy to reinforcement learning. The main positioning against prior performative prediction, strategic classification, and robust optimization remains; relocating related work is not a new literature contribution.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: most detailed related work moves from Section 5 to Appendix B, contributions become a dedicated subsection, and takeaways and a standalone conclusion are added. Extensive editing of explanations and proofs accompanies the restructuring.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a conference layout with two-column main text and references, revised typography, running headers, and reformatted equations and tables. The same figures are resized and repositioned, and captions are edited, including an explicit sample count in Figure 2. The change is primarily presentation rather than new visual evidence.

improvement.justification: v3 improves explicit assumptions and the shift-recursion argument, but revisions are not consistently propagated. Theorem 3.7 and its proof use different iteration exponents; Appendix C.2 evaluates the revised 1/ν sampling term as a square root despite ν=4. The semi-simulation also retains a 95% claim at δ=0.05 although Theorem 3.13 now guarantees 1−3δ. These conflicts affect central guarantees and their illustration, preventing a reliable judgment of net quality improvement.
